name: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease
aliases: idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis

reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A true idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in the growing child, not a traction apophysitis
Affected bone is the femoral head (capital femoral epiphysis) of the hip
Typically affects children roughly four to eight years of age, and is several times more common in boys, usually unilateral
Presents with a painless or mildly painful limp and referred pain to the groin, thigh or knee, with restricted hip abduction and internal rotation
The radiographic hallmark evolves from a smaller, denser epiphysis and a subchondral crescent fracture line through fragmentation to reossification and residual deformity
The lateral pillar (Herring) and Catterall classifications describe the extent of femoral head involvement and guide prognosis
Knee or thigh pain in a young child should always prompt examination of the hip to avoid missing the diagnosis
Management centres on maintaining hip motion and femoral head containment using activity modification, physiotherapy, bracing or containment surgery as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is an idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis caused by interruption of its blood supply in the immature hip. The precarious vascular supply of the developing femoral head, dependent largely on the lateral epiphyseal vessels, undergoes one or more episodes of ischaemia, leading to death of the subchondral bone and marrow. The necrotic bone becomes mechanically weak, and a subchondral fracture may occur followed by fragmentation and resorption. Revascularisation and creeping substitution then rebuild the epiphysis, but during this vulnerable phase the softened femoral head can deform under load, producing flattening and enlargement (coxa plana and coxa magna). The ultimate shape of the femoral head and its congruency with the acetabulum determine long-term hip function.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the hip
Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia or spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia
Secondary osteonecrosis (for example from corticosteroids, sickle cell disease or Gaucher disease)
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis of the hip
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and frog-lateral pelvic radiographs to assess the epiphysis and stage the disease
Magnetic resonance imaging for early diagnosis before radiographic change and to assess femoral head coverage
Lateral pillar (Herring) classification to help predict outcome
Assessment of hip range of motion, particularly abduction and internal rotation
Bilateral imaging and consideration of an epiphyseal dysplasia if changes are symmetrical
Investigations for a secondary cause of osteonecrosis when the presentation is atypical
redFlags: Fever, systemic upset or a markedly irritable hip suggesting septic arthritis
Bilateral symmetrical epiphyseal changes indicating a skeletal dysplasia rather than Perthes disease
An acute inability to bear weight, which may signal slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Progressive femoral head extrusion and loss of containment during the fragmentation phase
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on age at onset, extent of femoral head involvement and residual head shape; younger children with limited involvement often remodel well, whereas older children with extensive involvement and an aspherical, incongruent head are at greater risk of premature osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Attributing a child's knee or thigh pain to a local cause and failing to examine and image the hip
Mistaking early Perthes disease for transient synovitis and not arranging follow-up
Overlooking bilateral symmetrical changes that indicate an epiphyseal dysplasia
Losing femoral head containment by neglecting range of motion during the vulnerable fragmentation phase
management: Base management on the principle of containment, keeping the femoral head within the acetabulum during the biologically plastic phase
In younger children with limited involvement, use non-operative care with activity modification, protected weight-bearing and simple analgesia
Maintain and restore hip movement, especially abduction and internal rotation, with physiotherapy and where needed an abduction orthosis
Consider containment surgery such as femoral varus or pelvic (acetabular) osteotomy for older children or those with extensive femoral head involvement
Provide symptomatic pain relief with anti-inflammatory agents during painful phases
Monitor with serial radiographs, staging progression and femoral head coverage (for example the lateral pillar classification) to guide treatment
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics with long-term follow-up for residual deformity and later risk of premature osteoarthritis requiring joint-preserving or replacement surgery
